methods.label: Count the overlap once
methods.explanation:
Adding the areas of the two squares counts their common region twice, so we must subtract that overlap once. In the displayed figure, \(A\) lies on \(GH\) and \(B\) lies on \(GF\); the overlap is triangle \(AGB\).

Each square has side length \(10\), so each has area \(10^2=100\). Since \(G\) is the center of square \(ABCD\), its perpendicular distance to side \(AB\) is half the side length, or \(5\). Using \(AB=10\) as the triangle's base gives
\[
\text{area of }AGB=\frac{10\cdot5}{2}=25.
\]
Subtracting this extra copy of the overlap, the area covered by the squares is
\[
100+100-25=\boxed{175},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
